standard_text: Solve equations of the form px + q = r and p(x + q) = r fluently, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Represent real-world problems using equations of these forms and solve such problems.

progression.narrative: This standard asks seventh graders to solve equations of the form px + q = r and p(x + q) = r fluently with rational numbers, and to write and solve equations of these forms from real-world situations. The on-grade skills build from solving the bare two-step equation, to handling the parentheses form, to identifying, writing, and finally comparing equivalent models of a situation. Students who stall here usually cannot yet undo an operation reliably or evaluate an expression in the right order, gaps that reach back to grades 3 through 5. Intervention should rebuild missing-number thinking and order of operations first, then the grade six skills of solving one-step equations and checking a value by substitution, and only then return to two-step solving.

steps.rationale: The mechanical core: solve a two-step equation px + q = r by undoing operations in reverse order. This is the Below-proficiency task and the procedure every later step relies on.

The standard's second equation form, p(x + q) = r, adds the parentheses. Students need a reliable route (divide first or distribute) and must multiply every term inside -- a distinct mechanic worth its own step.
Before writing an equation from scratch, students identify which equation matches a situation, mapping each number to its job. Recognizing the model is a separate skill from executing it.
The At-proficiency demand: write AND solve a real-world equation, first with whole numbers. Building the equation (often p(x + q) = r for a whole group) is distinct from solving it.
The same modeling with rational values (fractions and decimals), where the 'fluently, with rational numbers' demand bites -- students must finish by dividing out a fraction or decimal coefficient.
The Above-proficiency payoff: model one situation with more than one equivalent equation, compare algebraic and arithmetic methods, and judge whether a solution is reasonable.

skills.name: Find the missing number in an equation

prerequisite_skill.description: Use fact families and inverse operations to find the missing number in an addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division equation.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: What number goes in the box: [] + 7 = 15?

skills.i_do_script: A missing-number equation hides one number, and the other two point straight at it. Watch: [] + 7 = 15. On a number line I stand at 15 and the 7 was a jump forward, so I jump 7 back and land on 8. Check: 8 + 7 = 15. Now 8 x [] = 40. The fact family for 8 and 40 says 40 divided by 8 is 5, so the box is 5. Addition and subtraction undo each other, and so do multiplication and division. I always check by putting my number back in the box.

canonical_error.pattern: Combines the two given numbers with the operation shown instead of undoing it
canonical_error.example: For [] + 7 = 15 the student adds 7 and 15 and writes 22
canonical_error.why: The student treats the equation as a computation prompt instead of a riddle. The 7 was already added to the hidden number, so you take it back off: 15 - 7 = 8. The check exposes it: 22 + 7 is not 15.

skills.item_template: A one-operation missing-number equation with whole numbers ([] + q = r, [] - q = r, p x [] = r, or [] / p = r), facts within grade 4 range. Student finds the missing number. Short response fluency bank.

redirect_script.stop: Is the box asking you to compute, or to undo?
redirect_script.prompt: The equation already did something to the hidden number. Jump BACKWARD on the number line, or use the fact family: if adding 7 got you to 15, subtracting 7 gets you back. Then check by putting your answer in the box.
redirect_script.praise: You went backward to find the hidden number and your check proved it.

vocabulary.definition: A set of related facts using the same three numbers, like 8 + 7 = 15, 15 - 7 = 8, and 15 - 8 = 7.
The hidden number in an equation, often shown as a box or blank.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 3 and 4 fact families with fact triangles and number-line jumps.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a number line from 0 to 20. Mark 15. Draw the [] + 7 = 15 story as a jump of 7 that LANDS on 15, starting from a mystery spot.
The jump forward was 7 and it landed on 15. How do we find where it started?
Jump 7 backward from 15 and land on 8. The missing number is 8, because 8 + 7 = 15. Undoing the jump finds the start.
If a student says 22, walk the jump on the line: does starting at 22 and jumping 7 forward land on 15?
Your turn: [] - 6 = 9. Which way do you jump to get back to the start?

skills.name: Evaluate expressions with parentheses using the order of operations

prerequisite_skill.description: Evaluate a whole-number expression that has parentheses, doing the grouped part first and multiplying before adding.

skills.i_do_script: Parentheses are a basket: whatever is inside gets bundled first, and the number outside acts on the whole basket. Watch: 4 x (3 + 2). The basket holds 3 + 2 = 5, and I have 4 baskets of 5, so 20. Compare that to 4 x 3 + 2 with no basket: multiplication goes first, 12 + 2 = 14. Different answers, because the basket changes what the 4 multiplies. Inside the parentheses first, then multiply or divide, then add or subtract.

canonical_error.pattern: Ignores the parentheses and works left to right, or lets the outside number reach only the first number inside
canonical_error.example: For 4 x (3 + 2) the student computes 4 x 3 = 12, then + 2, and writes 14
canonical_error.why: The student multiplied the 4 by only the 3, but the parentheses bundle 3 + 2 into one amount of 5. The 4 baskets each hold 5 counters, so the total is 20, not 14.

skills.item_template: A whole-number expression with one set of parentheses (sums and products within grade 5 range). Student evaluates it. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Which is greater: 3 x (4 + 2) or 3 x 4 + 2?
sample_items.answer: 3 x (4 + 2), because it equals 18 and 3 x 4 + 2 equals 14

redirect_script.prompt: Do the parentheses first: bundle what is inside into one number. Then the number outside acts on that whole bundle, not just the first thing in it.
redirect_script.praise: You bundled the basket first, so the outside number reached everything inside.

vocabulary.definition: Grouping symbols that bundle part of an expression to be done first.
The agreed order for evaluating: parentheses first, then multiply or divide, then add or subtract.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 5 order of operations with basket and array pictures.

worked_example_script.text: Draw 4 baskets. In each basket put 3 red counters and 2 blue counters.
How many counters are in ONE basket? So how many in all 4 baskets?
Each basket holds 3 + 2 = 5 counters, and 4 baskets of 5 make 20. That is 4 x (3 + 2) = 20. Writing 4 x 3 + 2 = 14 counts the blue counters from only one basket.
If a student says 14, point at the picture: how many blue counters are really on the table?
Your turn: draw or picture 2 x (5 + 6). What is in each basket, and what is the total?

skills.name: Solve one-step equations of the form x + p = q and px = q

prerequisite_skill.description: Solve a one-step equation by applying the inverse operation to both sides, with whole numbers and simple positive fractions and decimals.

skills.i_do_script: An equation is a balanced scale, and one thing has been done to x. To get x alone I undo that one thing on BOTH sides so the scale stays level. Watch: x + 9 = 17. Nine was added, so I subtract 9 from both sides: x = 8. Check: 8 + 9 = 17. Now 6x = 42. Here x is multiplied by 6, so I divide both sides by 6: x = 7. Check: 6 x 7 = 42. Name what happened to x, do the opposite to both sides, then check.

canonical_error.pattern: Applies the operation shown instead of its inverse, or changes only one side
canonical_error.example: For x + 9 = 17 the student adds 9 to 17 and writes x = 26
canonical_error.why: The student repeats the visible operation instead of undoing it. The 9 is already on x's side, so it must come OFF: subtract 9 from both sides. The check catches it: 26 + 9 is not 17.

skills.item_template: A one-step equation (x + p = q, x - p = q, px = q, or x/p = q) with nonnegative rational numbers, at most one simple fraction or decimal. Student isolates x. Numeric or MC response.

sample_items.stem:
An equation is given.

  x + 9 = 17

What is the solution to the equation?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Subtract 9 from both sides: x = 8. '26' adds 9 instead of subtracting; '9' copies the constant; '153' multiplies 9 by 17.

sample_items.stem: Solve x - 5 = 12.

An equation is given.

  5x = 35

What is the solution to the equation?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Divide both sides by 5: x = 7. '30' subtracts 5; '40' adds 5; '175' multiplies by 5 instead of dividing.

sample_items.stem: Solve x/3 = 8.
Solve 6x = 42.
Solve x + 2.5 = 7.
Solve 4x = 10.
Solve x + 3/4 = 2.

redirect_script.stop: What ONE thing happened to x?
redirect_script.prompt: Name it out loud: added, subtracted, multiplied, or divided. Then do the opposite to BOTH sides so the scale stays balanced, and check by substituting your answer back.
redirect_script.praise: You named the operation, undid it on both sides, and your check proved the answer.

vocabulary.definition: The operation that undoes another: subtraction undoes addition, division undoes multiplication.
The value of the variable that makes the equation true.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a balanced pan scale. On the left pan put a bag labeled x and 9 loose counters. On the right pan put 17 counters.
We want the bag alone on the left. What can we remove, and what must we do to keep the scale level?
Take 9 counters off the LEFT and 9 off the RIGHT. The bag now balances 8 counters, so x = 8. Check: 8 + 9 = 17.
If a student removes counters from only one side, tip the drawn scale: what happens to the balance?
Your turn: 6x = 42 means 6 identical bags balance 42 counters. How many counters in one bag?

practice_problems.stem: What operation undoes adding 6?
Solve x + 4 = 11.
Solve x - 8 = 15.
Solve 7x = 56.
Solve x + 1.5 = 6.
Solve x/5 = 6.
Solve 2.5x = 15.
Leo solved x + 8 = 20. Find his mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: Leo added 8 again instead of undoing it. Subtract 8 from both sides: x = 12. Check: 12 + 8 = 20.

activities.title: Bag and Balance
materials: A drawn or real pan balance mat
activities.instructions:
1. Partner A secretly puts counters in a bag and builds an equation on the balance mat, like bag + 9 counters on the left and 17 counters on the right.
2. Partner B removes the same number of loose counters from BOTH sides until the bag is alone.
3. Partner B says the solution; open the bag to check.
4. For px = q, use several identical bags on the left and share the right side equally among them.
5. Trade roles. Say each time: whatever leaves one side leaves the other.

activities.title: Undo Move Match-Up
materials: Card deck: one card per equation, one card per undo move
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards face up.
2. Match each equation to the move that solves it, like x + 4 = 10 to 'subtract 4 from both sides.'
3. To claim a match, state the solution and show the check out loud.
4. Two decoy cards name a wrong move; set them aside and explain why they fail.

strategy_links.why: Bags and a pan balance make 'undo the same thing on both sides' visible before the inverse-operation rule is named.
The repeat-the-operation error is stable and predictable; finding and fixing it in worked examples confronts it directly.
A choral routine of 'name the operation, do the opposite, both sides' hard-wires the solve habit.

questioning_prompts: What one thing is happening to x?
What move undoes that, and why must it happen on both sides?
How do you know the scale is still balanced after your move?
How can you prove your answer is right?
What would the check show if you had added instead of subtracted?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student applies the operation shown instead of its inverse.
misconception_redirects.say: Point at the balance: the 9 is already ON x's side. Does adding more counters get the bag alone? Take 9 off both sides instead.
misconception_redirects.praise: You undid the operation instead of repeating it, that is the whole move.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student changes only one side of the equation.
misconception_redirects.say: Tip the scale: if 9 leaves the left but not the right, the pans no longer balance. Whatever leaves one side leaves the other.
misconception_redirects.praise: You kept both sides balanced, so the equation stayed true.

quick_checks.look_for: x = 8 by subtracting 6 from both sides. An answer of 20 signals the add-again error.
x = 5.5 by dividing both sides by 4. An answer of 18 signals subtracting instead of dividing.

steps.annotation: One thing happened to x: it was multiplied by 5.
Division undoes multiplication, and it must happen on both sides.
Forty shared into 5 equal bags is 8 per bag.
Substitute back; both sides match, so x = 8.
One thing happened to x: it was multiplied by 6.
Division undoes the multiplication on both sides.
State the value of x.
Check by substituting your answer back into 6x = 42.

sentence_starters: The one thing happening to x is ___, so I ___ both sides.
I checked by putting ___ back in, and both sides equal ___.

skills.name: Use substitution to decide whether a value makes an equation true

prerequisite_skill.description: Substitute a value for the variable, evaluate in the correct order, and decide whether the equation is true.

skills.i_do_script: A solution is a value that makes the equation TRUE, and substitution is the test. Watch: is x = 4 a solution of 3x + 2 = 14? I replace x with 4: 3 x 4 + 2. Multiply first: 12. Then add: 14. The left side equals the right side, so yes, x = 4 is a solution. Try x = 5 in the same equation: 3 x 5 + 2 = 17, not 14, so x = 5 is not. Substitute, evaluate in order, compare the two sides.

canonical_error.pattern: Substitutes correctly but evaluates out of order, adding before multiplying
canonical_error.example: Checking x = 5 in 2x + 3, the student computes 5 + 3 = 8 and then 2 x 8 = 16 instead of 2 x 5 + 3 = 13
canonical_error.why: The student reads left to right through the substituted numbers and grabs the addition first. In 2x + 3 the 2 is glued to x by multiplication, so 2 times 5 happens before the 3 is added.

skills.item_template: An equation of the form px + q = r or p(x + q) = r with a candidate value, or an expression to evaluate at a given value. Student substitutes, evaluates in order, and decides true or false. Yes/no with work, numeric, or MC response.

sample_items.stem: Is x = 4 a solution of 3x + 2 = 14?
Is x = 5 a solution of 2x + 1 = 12?
Which value of x makes x + 6 = 13 true?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 7 + 6 = 13. '19' adds 6 to 13 instead of testing; '6' copies the constant; '5' is a near miss that fails the check (5 + 6 = 11).

sample_items.stem: Evaluate 4x + 3 when x = 2.
Is x = 3 a solution of 5(x + 1) = 20?
Is x = 10 a solution of 2(x - 4) = 10?
Evaluate 2(x + 5) when x = 3.
Which value of x makes 4x = 22 true?

redirect_script.stop: Which operation is glued to x?
redirect_script.prompt: Substitute the value, then evaluate in order: parentheses first, multiplication before addition. Only after you have one number on each side do you compare and decide true or false.
redirect_script.praise: You multiplied before adding and compared both sides, that is a real check.

vocabulary.definition: Replace the variable with a specific value.
A value that makes the equation true when substituted.

worked_example_script.text: Build 3x + 2 with objects: 3 identical cups (each hiding the same secret number of counters) and 2 loose counters.
If each cup holds 4 counters, how many counters are on the table in all?
Three cups of 4 make 12, plus the 2 loose counters is 14. So when x = 4, the expression 3x + 2 equals 14, and the equation 3x + 2 = 14 is TRUE. x = 4 is a solution.
If a student computes 4 + 2 = 6 first and then 3 x 6 = 18, point at the cups: are the 2 loose counters inside any cup?
Your turn: with the same cups, is x = 5 a solution of 3x + 2 = 14?

practice_problems.stem: Evaluate 2x + 1 when x = 3.
Evaluate 5x when x = 4.
Is x = 6 a solution of 4x - 3 = 21?
Is x = 2 a solution of 3(x + 4) = 18?
Is x = 9 a solution of 2x + 5 = 21?
Which makes 6x + 2 = 32 true: x = 3 or x = 5?
Test x = 4, x = 4.5, and x = 5 in 2x + 3 = 12. Which one is the solution?
practice_problems.answer: x = 4.5, because 2 x 4.5 + 3 = 12; the others give 11 and 13

practice_problems.stem: Mia checked whether x = 5 is a solution of 2x + 3 = 13. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: 2 x 8 = 16, so x = 5 is not a solution
practice_problems.answer: Mia added before multiplying. The 2 is glued to x, so multiply first: 2 x 5 = 10, then 10 + 3 = 13. Both sides match, so x = 5 IS a solution.

activities.title: Cups and Counters Check
activities.instructions:
1. Draw an equation card and a value card, like 3x + 2 = 14 with x = 4.
2. Build the left side: one cup per x, loose counters for the added constant.
3. Put the value in every cup, then count the total on the table.
4. Compare the count to the right side: match means solution, no match means not.
5. Say each time: cups first, loose counters after.

activities.title: Solution or Not?
activities.instructions:
1. Each card pairs an equation with a candidate value, like 'x = 4 in 3x + 2 = 14.'
2. Substitute and evaluate in order, showing the arithmetic on a whiteboard.
3. Sort the card into 'Solution' or 'Not a solution.'
4. The group must agree on the substituted arithmetic before a card is placed.
5. Debrief: which cards trick people who add before multiplying?

strategy_links.why: Cups for x and loose counters for the constant make 'multiply before adding' physical before the order rule is named.
Thinking aloud 'the 2 is glued to x, so multiply first' makes the invisible order choice audible and checkable.
The add-first evaluation error is precise and baitable, ideal for find-and-fix work.

questioning_prompts: What does it mean for a value to be a solution?
After you substitute, which operation happens first, and why?
What number did each side become? Do they match?
If the sides do not match, what does that tell you about the value?
How is checking p(x + q) different from checking px + q?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student adds the constant before multiplying the coefficient.
misconception_redirects.say: Look at the cups: the 2 loose counters are not inside any cup. Multiply the cups out first, then add the loose counters.
misconception_redirects.praise: You multiplied first and added after, so the value came out true.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student evaluates one side but never compares it to the other.
misconception_redirects.say: A check has two sides. Write what the left side became, write the right side, and say whether they match.
misconception_redirects.praise: You compared both sides, that is what decides solution or not.

quick_checks.look_for: Yes: 4 x 3 + 1 = 13. An answer of 16 (from 3 + 1 first) signals the order error.
14, doing the parentheses first: 2 x 7. An answer of 11 means the 2 reached only the x.

steps.annotation: Replace x with 4 everywhere it appears.
The 3 is glued to x by multiplication, so it goes before the addition.
The left side becomes one number.
Both sides match, so x = 4 makes the equation true.
Replace x with 3.
The coefficient multiplies before the constant is added.
Finish the addition on the left side.
Compare the two sides and decide true or false.

sentence_starters: I substituted ___ for x, and the left side became ___.
The sides ___ match, so x = ___ ___ a solution.

skills.name: Solve two-step equations of the form px + q = r
skills.i_do_script: An equation is a machine that ran forward on x, and solving is walking back out the way you came in -- the last door you entered is the first door you exit. Trace the machine before reaching for a rule. A two-step equation has TWO things happening to x, and I undo them in reverse order -- like taking off shoes before socks. Watch the spec's example: 3x - 6 = 27. The x is multiplied by 3, then 6 is subtracted. I clear the subtraction FIRST: add 6 to both sides, giving 3x = 33. Then I undo the multiplication: divide both sides by 3, giving x = 11. I finish by checking: 3(11) - 6 = 33 - 6 = 27. It works, so x = 11.

canonical_error.pattern: Undoes the multiplication before clearing the added or subtracted constant
canonical_error.example: For 3x - 6 = 27 the student divides by 3 first (getting x - 2 = 9) instead of adding 6 first
canonical_error.why: The student attacks the coefficient before the constant, following left-to-right habits instead of reverse order of operations. The added/subtracted term must be cleared before the multiplication is undone.

skills.item_template: A two-step equation px + q = r with integer (or simple rational) values. Student isolates x. MC or short numeric response.

sample_items.stem:
An equation is given.

  3x - 6 = 27

What is the solution to the equation?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Add 6 (33), divide by 3 -> 11. '7' comes from 21/3 (subtracting wrong); '36' keeps 3x = 36 without dividing; '66' doubles instead of dividing.

sample_items.stem:
An equation is given.

  4x + 5 = 25

What is the solution to the equation?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Subtract 5 (20), divide by 4 -> 5. '6.25' divides 25/4 without clearing +5; '7.5' uses 30/4; '100' multiplies.

sample_items.stem: Solve 7x - 3 = 18.
Solve 2x + 5 = 17.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- what is done to x LAST?
redirect_script.prompt: Sketch the machine doors again: which door did x pass through LAST on the way in? Undo in reverse: clear the added or subtracted number FIRST (do the opposite to both sides), and only THEN divide by the number multiplying x. Underline the constant and deal with it first.
redirect_script.praise: You cleared the constant before touching the coefficient -- that's the right order.

vocabulary.definition: An equation that needs two inverse operations to solve, like 3x - 6 = 27.
The number multiplied by the variable, like the 3 in 3x.
A plain number with no variable, like the -6 in 3x - 6.

worked_example_script.text: Draw the forward machine for 5x + 2 = 17: x goes in, passes through the 'times 5' door, then the '+ 2' door, and comes out as 17.
To walk BACK from 17 to x, which door do you exit through first -- the '+ 2' door or the 'times 5' door? And what is the undo of + 2?

You leave through the LAST door first: subtract 2 to get back to 15, then undo the 'times 5' door by dividing, landing on x = 3. Exiting the 'times 5' door first shoves the +2 through a division it never went through going in.
Write '5x + 2 = 17.'
What two things are happening to x, and in what order?
x is times 5, then + 2. Clear the +2 first: subtract 2 to get 5x = 15. Then divide by 5: x = 3.
If the student divides by 5 first, ask 'what number is added to the 5x? Clear that first.'
Your turn: 3x - 6 = 27. Which do you undo first?

practice_problems.stem: Solve x + 4 = 10.
In 3x - 6 = 27, which do you undo first: the '- 6' or the 'times 3'?
Solve 3x - 6 = 27.
practice_problems.notes: The spec's Below example; add 6, then divide by 3.

practice_problems.stem: Solve 4x + 5 = 25.
Alex solved 2x + 8 = 20. Find and fix the mistake.
practice_problems.answer: Alex divided by 2 before clearing the + 8. Clear the constant first: 2x = 12, then divide by 2 to get x = 6. Check: 2(6) + 8 = 20.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: dividing before subtracting.

practice_problems.stem: Solve 7x - 3 = 18.
Solve 4x + 3 = 1.
practice_problems.notes: Rational, negative solution: 4x = -2.

practice_problems.stem: Write a two-step equation of the form px + q = r whose solution is x = 4. Show your check.
practice_problems.notes: Reverse direction -- build an equation with a known solution.

activities.title: Which Step First?
materials: Card set: 8 equations (some one-step, some two-step)
activities.instructions:
1. Each card shows an equation like 3x - 6 = 27.
2. Decide the FIRST move: 'Add or subtract first' or 'Divide first.'
3. Sort every card -- a two-step equation always clears the constant first; a one-step (like 5x = 30) only divides.
4. Then solve three cards and check by substituting back.
5. Debrief: what goes wrong if you divide before clearing the constant?

activities.title: Order Detective
activities.instructions:
1. Read Alex's solution to 2x + 8 = 20.
2. Circle the exact line where Alex undid the wrong operation first.
3. Redo the solve in the correct order and check your answer.
4. Write the rule: which do you always clear first -- the constant or the coefficient?

content.worked_problem: 2x + 8 = 20. Alex divided by 2 first and got x = 2.
content.error_step: Alex divided by 2 before clearing the + 8.
content.why: Clear the added constant first: 2x = 12, then divide by 2 to get x = 6.

strategy_links.why: Two-step solving is a fixed procedure; gradual release adds one inverse-operation move at a time before independent practice.
The divide-before-subtract slip is a precise, baitable error ideal for find-and-fix.
Choral response on 'clear the constant first, then divide' hard-wires the reverse-order habit.

questioning_prompts: What two things are happening to x, and in what order?
Which do you undo first -- and why that one?
What do you get after you clear the constant?
How can you check that your answer is right?
Where would dividing too early show up in your answer?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides by the coefficient before clearing the added or subtracted constant.
misconception_redirects.say: Undo in reverse: clear the added or subtracted number FIRST (do the opposite to both sides), and only THEN divide by the number multiplying x. Underline the constant and deal with it first.
misconception_redirects.praise: You cleared the constant before touching the coefficient -- that's the right order.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student changes only one side of the equation.
misconception_redirects.say: Whatever you do to one side, do to the other. Write the '+ 6' under BOTH sides so the equation stays balanced.
misconception_redirects.praise: You kept both sides balanced -- that's what keeps the equation true.

quick_checks.look_for: x = 3 (subtract 2, then divide by 5). Dividing first (17/5 = 3.4) signals the order error.
x = 3 (add 1, then divide by 4). An answer of 2.75 means the student divided before adding.

sentence_starters: First I undo the ___ by ___ing both sides, which gives ___.
Then I divide both sides by ___ to get x = ___.

steps.annotation: Two operations on x: times 2, then + 5.
Clear the added constant first, on both sides.
Undo the multiplication last.
Substitute back -- both sides match, so x = 6.
Two operations: times 4, then - 7.
Clear the constant first (add 7 to both sides).
Divide both sides by 4 to isolate x.
Check by substituting your answer into the original.

skills.name: Solve equations of the form p(x + q) = r
skills.i_do_script: 4(x + 3) means FOUR full copies of everything in the parentheses -- four x's and four 3s sitting on the table. See all the copies before any arrow rule. When the variable sits inside parentheses, p(x + q) = r, I have two good routes. Watch the spec's example: 0.5(x - 3) = 7.5. Route 1 -- divide first: divide both sides by 0.5 to get x - 3 = 15, then add 3 to get x = 18. Route 2 -- distribute first: 0.5 times x is 0.5x and 0.5 times -3 is -1.5, giving 0.5x - 1.5 = 7.5, then add 1.5 and divide by 0.5 to get x = 18. Both land on x = 18. The trap in distributing is forgetting to multiply the SECOND number inside, so I say both products out loud.

canonical_error.pattern: Distributes p to the variable only, forgetting to multiply the constant inside the parentheses
canonical_error.example: For 0.5(x - 3) = 7.5 the student writes 0.5x - 3 = 7.5 (never multiplied -3 by 0.5) instead of 0.5x - 1.5 = 7.5
canonical_error.why: The student treats the outside factor as attached to just the first term. The distributive property multiplies EVERY term inside: p(x + q) = px + pq. Missing the second product corrupts the solve.

skills.item_template: An equation p(x + q) = r with rational p, q, r (at least one may be a fraction or decimal). Student solves by dividing first or distributing first. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem:
An equation is given.

  0.5(x - 3) = 7.5

What is the solution to the equation?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Divide by 0.5 -> x - 3 = 15, add 3 -> 18. Distributing to only the first term (0.5x - 3 = 7.5) would give x = 21.

sample_items.stem: Solve 3(x + 5) = 27.

skills.i_do_script: Draw the total as one money bar: the one-time fee is a chunk you peel off the end, and what remains is still MONEY that the per-item price must chop into cases. Watch the spec's example: a baker uses 3 cups of flour for bread and 1.5 cups for each batch of cookies, using 12 cups total. The 1.5 is per batch, so it multiplies x: 1.5x; the 3 cups is a one-time amount: + 3; the total is 12. So 1.5x + 3 = 12. I subtract 3 to get 1.5x = 9, then divide by 1.5 to get x = 6 batches. Dividing by 1.5 is the step people skip -- I never leave the coefficient attached.

activities.title: Set Up, Then Finish the Divide
activities.instructions:
1. Draw a context card with a fraction or decimal rate (like the baker's 1.5 cups).
2. In 'Set up,' write the equation (rate times x plus one-time amount = total).
3. In 'Solve,' clear the constant, THEN divide by the fraction/decimal coefficient -- you may use a calculator.
4. Circle the final answer only after x stands alone, and check by substituting back.
5. Debrief: what is the last step people forget when the coefficient is a decimal?

activities.title: Finish the Divide
activities.instructions:
1. Read Jamie's solve of 1.5x + 3 = 12 that ends at 'x = 9.'
2. Ask: after 1.5x = 9, is x by itself yet?
3. Do the missing step (divide by 1.5) and check your answer.
4. Write a reminder for yourself about decimal or fraction coefficients.

content.error_step: Jamie stopped without dividing by the 1.5 still multiplying x.
content.why: Divide both sides by 1.5: x = 6. A calculator is allowed, so there is no excuse to skip the divide.

strategy_links.why: The stopped-early (no final divide) error is precise and common with decimal coefficients -- ideal for find-and-fix.
Thinking aloud 'is x by itself yet?' models the self-check that catches the missing divide.
Gradual release lets students set up first, then practice finishing the rational-coefficient divide independently.

questioning_prompts: Which number is per unit (the coefficient), and which is one-time?
After you clear the constant, is x by itself yet?
What do you divide both sides by to finish?
Would a calculator help you trust the decimal step?
Does your answer make sense as a count in this story?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student clears the constant but leaves x multiplied by a decimal or fraction.
misconception_redirects.say: After you clear the constant, look at the number stuck to x. If it is a fraction or decimal, divide BOTH sides by it (a calculator is allowed). Only x, alone, means you are finished.
misconception_redirects.praise: You divided out the decimal coefficient -- that's the last step people skip.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student mishandles the decimal arithmetic (e.g., 67.5 - 5 wrong).
misconception_redirects.say: Slow the arithmetic down and use the calculator you are allowed. Line up the decimals: 67.5 - 5 = 62.5.
misconception_redirects.praise: You kept the decimal arithmetic accurate -- fluency includes trusting the numbers.

quick_checks.look_for: x = 4 (2.5x = 10, then divide by 2.5). Stopping at 2.5x = 10 and saying x = 10 is the missing-divide error.

quick_checks.look_for: m = 8 (0.5m = 4, divide by 0.5). An answer of 4 means the student skipped dividing by 0.5.

After I subtract ___, x is still times ___, so I divide to get x = ___.

steps.annotation: 1.5 cups per batch times x, plus 3 cups for bread, equals 12.
Clear the one-time amount first.
x was multiplied by 1.5, so divide both sides by 1.5 (a calculator is allowed).
6 batches -- the total checks.

Clear the one-time shipping first.
x is still times 7.5 -- divide both sides by 7.5.

skills.name: Represent a problem with more than one equivalent equation and compare methods
skills.i_do_script: At the top level I can model ONE situation with more than one correct equation and know they are equivalent, and I can judge whether an answer is reasonable. Watch the spec's example: a shopper buys 5 red shirts and x blue shirts, each $9.50, for $76. One equation groups all the shirts: 9.50(x + 5) = 76. Another distributes the price: 9.50x + 47.50 = 76. Both are correct because distributing 9.50(x + 5) gives 9.50x + 47.50 -- same equation, different form. Both solve to x = 3. To judge reasonableness I check: 3 blue plus 5 red is 8 shirts at $9.50 is $76. It fits.

canonical_error.pattern: Treats the grouped and distributed forms as different equations, or distributes incorrectly so the two forms are not truly equivalent
canonical_error.example: Calls 9.50(x + 5) = 76 and 9.50x + 5 = 76 equivalent -- the second forgot to multiply 5 by 9.50 (it should be 47.50)
canonical_error.why: The student does not connect p(x + q) with px + pq, or distributes only the first term. Two equations are equivalent only when one distributes exactly into the other and both share the same solution.

skills.item_template: A real-world situation; student writes or selects TWO equivalent equations, compares two solution methods, or judges whether a stated solution is reasonable. Multiple-select or multi-part response.

sample_items.stem: A shopper buys 5 red shirts and x blue shirts at $9.50 each for $76. Write the TWO equivalent equations that model this.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The grouped form 9.50(x + 5) = 76 distributes exactly into 9.50x + 47.50 = 76. '9.50x + 5 = 76' forgets to multiply the 5 by 9.50, so it is NOT equivalent.

sample_items.stem: A booth sells x student tickets and 4 adult tickets at $7 each for $84 total. Write two equivalent equations for x, then solve.
A linear equation is 3(x - 2) = 9. Student A distributes first; Student B divides both sides by 3 first. Do the two methods give the same solution? Solve both ways.
A student solved 5(x + 2) = 45 and got x = 11. Is that reasonable? Check it and correct it if needed.
sample_items.answer: No -- 5(11 + 2) = 5(13) = 65, not 45. The correct solution is x = 7, since 5(7 + 2) = 5(9) = 45.

redirect_script.stop: Are those two equations really the same?
redirect_script.prompt: Distribute the grouped form on scratch paper: p(x + q) becomes px + pq. If your two equations don't match after distributing -- or don't share the same solution -- they aren't equivalent. Check that every term got multiplied.
redirect_script.praise: You showed the two forms distribute into each other AND share a solution -- truly equivalent.

vocabulary.definition: Equations with the same solution; one distributes exactly into the other.
Multiply the outside factor by every term inside the parentheses.
An answer that actually fits the situation when you check it.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 8.AF.1 (multi-step equations, variables on both sides).

worked_example_script.text: Write 'A team buys x new balls and 3 spares at $6 each, $54 total.'
What is one equation that groups all the balls?
6(x + 3) = 54. Distribute it: 6x + 18 = 54 -- a second, equivalent equation. Both solve to x = 6.
If a student writes 6x + 3 = 54, ask 'what is 6 times 3?'
Your turn: 5 red and x blue shirts at $9.50, total $76 -- write both forms.

Distribute: 9.50(x + 5).
A shopper buys 5 red shirts and x blue shirts at $9.50 each for $76. Write the TWO equivalent equations that model this.
practice_problems.notes: Spec's Above example; grouped and distributed forms.

practice_problems.stem: 3(x - 2) = 9. Student A distributes first; Student B divides by 3 first. Do they get the same solution? Solve both ways.
practice_problems.notes: Spec's Above compare-methods item.

practice_problems.stem: Riley says 6(x + 3) = 48 and 6x + 3 = 48 are the same equation. Find and fix the error.
shown_work: Riley wrote: '6(x + 3) = 48 is the same as 6x + 3 = 48.'
practice_problems.answer: Distributing 6(x + 3) gives 6x + 18, not 6x + 3. The equivalent form is 6x + 18 = 48, which solves to x = 5 (matching 6(x + 3) = 48). Riley multiplied only the first term.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: incomplete distribution breaks equivalence.

practice_problems.stem: A booth sells x student tickets and 4 adult tickets at $7 each for $84. Write two equivalent equations, then solve.
practice_problems.notes: Both forms, then solve.

practice_problems.stem: A number is multiplied by 4, then 6 is added, giving 30. Solve it algebraically (write an equation) and arithmetically (work backward). Which operations does each method use, and in what order?
practice_problems.answer: Algebraic: 4x + 6 = 30 -> 4x = 24 -> x = 6. Arithmetic: undo the +6 (30 - 6 = 24), then undo the times 4 (24 / 4 = 6). Both use subtraction then division, in the same order.
practice_problems.notes: Compare algebraic and arithmetic approaches (Above descriptor).

practice_problems.notes: Judge reasonableness and correct (Above descriptor).

activities.title: Same Equation, Two Forms
materials: Card set: 6 grouped-form cards and 8 distributed-form cards (two incomplete-distribution decoys)
activities.instructions:
1. Match each grouped form p(x + q) to its correct distributed form.
2. Two distributed cards are decoys that multiplied only the first term -- set them aside and name why they are NOT equivalent.
3. To claim a match, show that distributing gives every term.
4. Pick one matched pair and solve both forms to confirm the same answer.
5. Debrief: what has to be true for two equations to be equivalent?

activities.title: Is It Really Equivalent?
activities.instructions:
1. Read Riley's claim that 6(x + 3) = 48 and 6x + 3 = 48 are the same.
2. Distribute 6(x + 3) fully -- what should the constant term be?
3. Solve both of Riley's equations and show their solutions differ.
4. Write the two-part test for equivalence: distributes exactly AND same solution.

content.error_step: Riley multiplied 6 by x but not by the 3 inside.
content.why: 6(x + 3) = 6x + 18, so the equivalent form is 6x + 18 = 48 (x = 5). Riley's 6x + 3 = 48 gives x = 7.5 -- a different equation.

strategy_links.why: Comparing a correct equivalence against an incomplete-distribution version is exactly a correct-vs-incorrect worked-example routine.
The false-equivalence error is a precise, high-value mistake for a find-and-fix routine.
Writing WHY two forms are equivalent (or why an answer is reasonable) cements the justification the Above band demands.

questioning_prompts: What is one equation that groups everything? What is another that distributes it?
How can you PROVE two equations are equivalent?
Do both solution methods land on the same answer?
Is the answer reasonable -- does it fit the situation when you check?
Which method was more efficient here, and why?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student treats a grouped form and an incompletely distributed form as equivalent.
misconception_redirects.say: Distribute the grouped form on scratch paper: p(x + q) becomes px + pq. If your two equations don't match after distributing -- or don't share the same solution -- they aren't equivalent. Check that every term got multiplied.
misconception_redirects.praise: You showed the two forms distribute into each other AND share a solution -- truly equivalent.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student accepts an answer without judging whether it is reasonable.
misconception_redirects.say: Put the answer back into the story and check the total. If the numbers don't fit -- like paying more than the total -- the answer isn't reasonable.
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked the answer against the situation -- that's judging reasonableness.

quick_checks.look_for: 8x + 16. Writing 8x + 2 (forgetting to multiply the 2) is the equivalence-breaking error.

quick_checks.prompt: A student says x = 10 solves 4(x + 1) = 24. Reasonable?
quick_checks.look_for: No -- 4(11) = 44, not 24; the correct x = 5. A 'yes' means they didn't check.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S4, writing and solving a real-world equation, the At-proficiency core. If they pass, push to S5 (rational-number contexts) and S6 (equivalent equations and reasonableness). If they fail, drop below grade level: B1 checks one-step equation solving and B2 checks substitution and order of operations, the two grade 6 skills two-step solving leans on. If those wobble, the foundations F1 (missing-number equations) and F2 (parentheses and order of operations) locate the gap in grades 3 through 5. S1, S2, and S3 remain available to probe the standard's own solving and modeling mechanics.
